title: Understanding Memory Requirements for LLM Inference
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 16)
In the previous part, I explored:

llama.cpp
GGUF
quantized models
local CPU inference
That article helped me understand how smaller models can run on CPUs, local machines, and cloud CPU instances.
But once I started thinking more practically, another question became very important:

How much memory do we actually need
to run LLM inference?
At first, I used to think about this mainly as:
Can the model fit?
But that is only one part of the story.
For inference, memory is not only used by the model weights.
Memory is also used by:

KV cache
temporary compute buffers
activations
runtime overhead
framework overhead
OS memory
safety margin
So the real question is not just:
Can I load the model?
The better question is:

Can I load the model
and still have enough memory
for the actual inference workload?
That is what this article is about.
Why does memory planning matter?
When running LLM inference, memory decides many practical things.
It decides:

which model can load
how long the context can be
how many users can run at once
how many tokens can be generated
how large the batch can be
whether the system crashes or stays stable
This is why memory planning is one of the most important parts of inference.
A model may run fine for one request.
But when we increase:

context length
concurrent users
batch size
output tokens
the same model may suddenly fail.
That is because the memory requirement is not fixed.
It grows with the workload.
What memory are we talking about?
The word memory can mean different things depending on where inference is running.
For CPU inference:
memory = system RAM
For GPU inference:
memory = GPU VRAM / HBM
For Apple Silicon or unified memory systems, CPU and GPU may share memory.
But the high-level idea is the same.
The model and runtime need enough memory to hold everything required for inference.
What are the main memory components?
A simple formula is:

Total inference memory
=
model weights
+
KV cache
+
temporary compute memory
+
runtime overhead
+
safety margin
The two biggest pieces are usually:

model weights
+
KV cache
Weights decide whether the model can load.
KV cache decides how much context and concurrency the system can handle.
That distinction is very important.
What are model weights?
Model weights are the learned parameters of the model.
When we say:
7B model
we mean the model has roughly:
7 billion parameters
Each parameter is a number.
For example:
These numbers are stored in memory.
So the first memory calculation is simple:

model weight memory
=
number of parameters
×
bytes per parameter
How many bytes does each parameter need?
That depends on precision.
A rough guide:

FP32  = 4 bytes per parameter
FP16  = 2 bytes per parameter
BF16  = 2 bytes per parameter
INT8  ≈ 1 byte per parameter
INT4  ≈ 0.5 byte per parameter
So for a 7B model in FP16:

7 billion × 2 bytes
≈ 14 GB
That means the weights alone need roughly 14 GB.
But that does not mean a 16 GB machine is enough.
Because we still need memory for KV cache and runtime overhead.
What happens with quantized models?
Quantization stores model weights using fewer bits.
For example:

FP16 → 16 bits
INT8 → 8 bits
INT4 → 4 bits
So the rough memory estimate becomes:

7B FP16
≈ 14 GB

7B INT8
≈ 7 GB

7B INT4
≈ 3.5 GB
In practice, there is some extra metadata and format overhead.
So the exact number may not be perfectly equal to the simple formula.
For GGUF models, the easiest practical estimate is often:

model weight memory
≈
GGUF file size
That is not perfect, but it is a very useful starting point.
Why is this useful for CPU inference?
When using llama.cpp, I usually download a GGUF model.
Example:
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf
The file size gives a practical sense of how much memory the model weights need.
If the GGUF file is around 4.5 GB, then the system needs at least that much memory just for loading the model.
But again, that is only the starting point.
The full memory requirement is larger.
What is KV cache?
KV cache stores key and value tensors from previous tokens.
During generation, the model needs to attend to previous tokens.
Without KV cache, it would need to recompute a lot of previous attention information again and again.
KV cache avoids that.
The simple mental model is:

Prompt tokens create KV cache.

Generated tokens extend KV cache.

Longer sequence means larger KV cache.
So KV cache grows with the number of tokens being processed.
Why does KV cache matter so much?
Because KV cache grows with:

context length
number of active requests
number of layers
number of KV heads
head dimension
KV cache precision
This means memory usage increases when we increase:

longer prompts
longer generated outputs
more concurrent users
larger batch sizes
larger context windows
This is why KV cache is central to inference memory planning.
What is the KV cache formula?
A useful formula is:

KV cache memory
=
active sequences
×
tokens per sequence
×
number of layers
×
2
×
number of KV heads
×
head dimension
×
bytes per KV element
The 2 is because we store:

K cache
+
V cache
A more accurate version is:

KV cache memory
=
total active tokens
×
number of layers
×
2
×
number of KV heads
×
head dimension
×
bytes per KV element
This is the formula I want to remember.
What are active tokens?
Active tokens means all tokens currently stored in KV cache across active requests.
For one request:

active tokens
=
prompt tokens
+
generated tokens so far
For multiple requests:

total active tokens
=
request A tokens
+
request B tokens
+
request C tokens
+
...
So if we have:

Request A → 1000 tokens
Request B → 2000 tokens
Request C → 500 tokens
then:

total active tokens
=
3500 tokens
That total drives KV cache memory.
What is a simple KV cache example?
Suppose a model has:

number of layers = 32
number of KV heads = 8
head dimension = 128
KV cache dtype = FP16
FP16 means:
2 bytes per element
Now KV cache per token is:
That equals:
131,072 bytes
or roughly:
128 KB per token
That means every token for every active request needs around 128 KB of KV cache memory.
What does that mean for one request?
If one request uses a 4096-token context:
So one request may need around:
512 MB of KV cache
That is only KV cache.
It does not include model weights.
What about multiple active requests?
If we have 16 active requests, each using 4096 tokens:
Now KV cache alone is around:
8 GB
This is where inference memory becomes interesting.
A model may fit.
But the workload may not.
What does total memory look like?
Suppose:

model weights = 14 GB
KV cache = 8 GB
runtime overhead = 3 GB
Then total memory becomes:

14 GB
+
8 GB
+
3 GB
=
25 GB
So even though the model weights are only 14 GB, a 16 GB system would not be enough for this serving workload.
This is the key lesson.
What is the most important intuition?
The simplest intuition is:

Model weights decide if the model can load.

KV cache decides how much inference workload can run.
Or:

Weights are mostly fixed.

KV cache grows with users and tokens.
This is why memory planning for inference is not only about model size.
It is also about workload shape.
What is workload shape?
Workload shape means the kind of requests the system is serving.
For example:

short prompts
short outputs
few users
is very different from:

long prompts
long outputs
many users
Even if both use the same model, the memory requirements can be very different.
A chatbot with short messages may be manageable.
A document analysis system with long context may need much more memory.
Why does context length matter?
Context length directly affects KV cache.
If we increase context from:
4096 tokens
to:
8192 tokens
then KV cache roughly doubles.
If we increase it again to:
32768 tokens
then KV cache becomes much larger.
That means long-context inference can become memory-heavy very quickly.
This is why setting a large context window is not free.
Why does concurrency matter?
Concurrency means how many requests are active at the same time.
If one request needs 512 MB of KV cache, then:

1 request  → 512 MB
4 requests → 2 GB
8 requests → 4 GB
16 requests → 8 GB
So concurrency multiplies KV cache memory.
This is why serving many users requires much more memory than running one local prompt.
How does this connect to batching?
Batching improves throughput by processing multiple requests together.
But batching also means more active sequences.
More active sequences means more KV cache memory.
So batching creates a tradeoff:

larger batch
=
better GPU/CPU utilization
+
more KV cache memory
This connects directly to continuous batching.
Continuous batching tries to keep the active batch full.
But every active request needs KV cache.
So the scheduler must constantly balance:

compute utilization
vs
memory capacity
How does this connect to PagedAttention?
PagedAttention exists because KV cache memory is difficult to manage efficiently.
Requests have different lengths.
They start at different times.
They finish at different times.
They grow token by token.
So the memory system needs to handle dynamic KV cache allocation.
The core idea is:

Continuous batching
keeps compute busy.

PagedAttention
helps manage KV cache memory efficiently.
This is why memory planning connects directly to vLLM internals.
What about temporary compute memory?
Besides weights and KV cache, inference needs temporary memory.
This includes:

activations
attention workspace
logits
sampling buffers
runtime buffers
communication buffers
framework overhead
During inference, activations are much smaller than training because we do not store everything for backpropagation.
But they still matter.
They can become more noticeable during:

large prefill
large batch size
long prompts
multi-GPU communication
So we should not plan memory with zero overhead.
What is a practical safety margin?
A practical estimate is:

total memory
≈
weights
+
KV cache
+
10% to 30% overhead
For small local experiments, the overhead may be smaller or manageable.
For production systems, I would be more conservative.
I do not want to run memory at 99%.
Because once the system is near the limit, small changes can cause failures.
Examples:

slightly longer prompt
more concurrent requests
larger batch
different model format
larger tokenizer buffers
runtime allocation spike
can push the system over the edge.
How should I calculate memory for CPU inference?
For CPU inference with llama.cpp, a practical formula is:

Required RAM
≈
GGUF model size
+
KV cache memory
+
compute buffers
+
OS memory
+
safety margin
The easiest first estimate:

Required RAM
≈
GGUF file size
+
KV cache estimate
+
20% overhead
This is not perfect, but it is useful.
Then the real measurement should come from running the server and reading the logs.
What should I check in llama.cpp logs?
When starting llama-server, I should look for memory-related logs such as:

model buffer size
KV buffer size
compute buffer size
graph memory
backend buffer size
These logs are very useful because they show what the runtime actually allocated.
So the practical workflow becomes:

estimate memory first
start the server
read actual memory logs
compare estimate vs reality
adjust settings
benchmark again
This is how the concept becomes practical.
Which llama.cpp settings affect memory?
Important settings include:

model file
context size
parallel slots
batch size
ubatch size
KV cache type
GPU offload layers
thread count
For CPU inference, context size is especially important.
A larger context means more KV cache memory.
More parallel slots means more simultaneous sequences.
So even with the same model, changing these settings can change memory usage significantly.
What does context size mean practically?
If I set a very large context size, I am asking the runtime to support more tokens.
That requires more KV cache memory.
For example:
context size = 4096
uses less KV cache than:
context size = 32768
So I should not set context length much larger than what my workload actually needs.
Large context is useful, but it has a memory cost.
How does this connect to the LLM Inference Workbench?
This is exactly the kind of thing I want the workbench to help me understand.
For each experiment, I want to track:

model
quantization
GGUF size
CPU shape
RAM
context size
parallel slots
batch size
TTFT
tokens/sec
p95 latency
memory usage
Then I can compare experiments.
For example:

Experiment 1:
Qwen2.5 7B Q4_K_M
context 4096
parallel 1

Experiment 2:
same model
context 8192
parallel 1

Experiment 3:
same model
context 4096
parallel 4
Now I can observe how memory changes.
This is much better than guessing.
What should I compare first?
I would start with one model and change one variable.
Example:

same model
same CPU shape
different context sizes
Then compare:

memory usage
TTFT
tokens/sec
latency
stability
After that, I can compare quantization formats:

Q4_K_M
vs
Q8_0
Then compare model sizes:

1.5B
vs
7B
vs
14B
The important rule is:
change one variable at a time
Otherwise, the results become hard to understand.
How should I calculate memory for GPU inference?
For GPU inference, the formula is similar:

Required GPU memory
≈
model weights in VRAM
+
KV cache in VRAM
+
activation / workspace memory
+
runtime overhead
+
safety margin
But there is one extra consideration.
If the model is split across multiple GPUs, the weight memory may be divided.
For tensor parallelism:
each GPU stores part of the model weights
For pipeline parallelism:
each GPU group stores some layers
For data parallelism:
each replica stores its own copy
So multi-GPU memory planning depends on the parallelism strategy.
What happens with tensor parallelism?
Suppose a model needs 80 GB of weights.
If we use tensor parallelism across 4 GPUs, then roughly:

80 GB / 4
=
20 GB per GPU
for weights.
This is simplified, but it gives the intuition.
By sharding weights, each GPU has more remaining memory for KV cache. That can help support larger context or more active requests. But tensor parallelism also adds communication cost.
So memory improves, but communication becomes important.
What happens with data parallelism?
Data parallelism is different. If we create 4 replicas, each replica has its own model copy. So memory is not divided across replicas.
Instead:

Replica 1 → full model copy
Replica 2 → full model copy
Replica 3 → full model copy
Replica 4 → full model copy
Data parallelism helps concurrency because requests can be spread across replicas.
But each replica needs enough memory to run the model and KV cache for its assigned users.
What is the difference between fitting and serving?
This is a very important distinction.
Fitting means:
Can I load the model?
Serving means:

Can I load the model
and handle the expected workload?
A model may fit for one request.
But it may not serve many users.
That is because serving adds:

concurrency
longer KV cache
batching
runtime overhead
latency constraints
So when planning inference memory, I should not stop at:
model loaded successfully
That only proves the first step.
What is the simplest capacity planning process?
I can use this process:

1. Estimate model weight memory.

2. Estimate KV cache per token.

3. Estimate total active tokens.

4. Multiply KV per token by active tokens.

5. Add temporary and runtime overhead.

6. Add safety margin.

7. Run the actual system.

8. Compare estimate with real measurements.
This gives both a mental model and a practical workflow.
What is a simple example?
Suppose:

model weights = 8 GB
KV cache per token = 128 KB
max tokens per request = 4096
active requests = 8
overhead = 3 GB
First calculate KV per request:
Then calculate KV for 8 requests:
Now total memory:

8 GB weights
+
4 GB KV cache
+
3 GB overhead
=
15 GB
Then add safety margin.
If we add 20%:
So I would not choose a 16 GB system for this workload.
I would want something closer to:
24 GB or more
That gives space for overhead and variance.
Why can estimates be wrong?
Memory estimates can be wrong because real systems have details like:

alignment
metadata
quantization overhead
framework buffers
fragmentation
memory preallocation
backend-specific buffers
different KV cache dtypes
different attention implementations
So the formula is not meant to be perfect.
It is meant to help us reason before running.
The real answer still comes from measurement.
What metrics should I track?
For memory experiments, I want to track:

model file size
loaded model memory
KV cache memory
total process memory
available system memory
context size
parallel slots
batch size
TTFT
tokens/sec
p95 latency
failure point
The failure point is useful.
For example:

works at context 4096
works at context 8192
starts swapping at context 16384
fails at context 32768
That teaches more than a single successful run.
What does this teach about inference systems?
It teaches that inference is not just compute.
Inference is also memory management.
The system is constantly balancing:

model size
context length
concurrency
latency
throughput
memory capacity
This is why modern serving engines spend so much effort on:

KV cache management
continuous batching
PagedAttention
prefix caching
chunked prefill
routing
scheduling
The hard part is not only generating tokens.
The hard part is generating tokens efficiently for many different requests under limited memory.
How does this connect to CPU inference?
For CPU inference, memory planning helps answer:

Can this model run on this machine?
How large can the context be?
How many parallel requests can I support?
When does the system start swapping?
Which quantization is practical?
This is very relevant for my LLM Inference Workbench.
If I can automate experiments around these questions, I can learn much faster.
Instead of saying:
this model feels slow
I can say:

this model uses this much memory,
with this context size,
and produces this tokens/sec,
on this CPU shape.
That is a much better learning loop.
How does this connect to GPU inference?
For GPU inference, memory planning helps answer:

Can this model fit in VRAM?
How much KV cache can we support?
How many active requests can run?
Do we need tensor parallelism?
Do we need more replicas?
Do we need a smaller context limit?
Do we need quantization?
This is where memory planning becomes architecture planning.
If one GPU is not enough, we need multi-GPU inference.
If one replica is not enough, we need more replicas.
If routing needs to consider cache locality, we need smarter distributed serving.
And that leads toward systems like llm-d.
What is the key mental model?
The key mental model is:

Total memory
=
weights
+
KV cache
+
overhead
But the deeper intuition is:

Weights are the cost of loading the model.

KV cache is the cost of serving the workload.
So when someone asks:
How much memory do I need for this model?
the answer should be:

For what context length?
For how many active requests?
With what precision?
On CPU or GPU?
Using which runtime?
Because the model alone is not enough information.
What comes next?
Now that memory planning is clearer, the next topic becomes very natural.
Once we understand that inference memory depends on:

KV cache
context length
active requests
routing
replicas
scheduling
the next question is:

How do large systems manage this
across a Kubernetes cluster?
That leads to:
llm-d
Because llm-d is about distributed LLM inference.
It connects many ideas we have already discussed:

vLLM
Kubernetes
replicas
routing
KV-cache-aware scheduling
disaggregated serving
distributed inference
So the next article can move from:
How much memory does one inference system need?
to:

How do we distribute inference
across many systems intelligently?
That feels like the right next step.
